n: Tax collectors and notorious sinners crowd around to hear Jesus. People whom respectable society shunned feel welcome with Him.

f.g: Jewish tax collectors working for Rome, widely viewed as traitors and cheats.

n: The religious leaders grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and even eats with them — sharing a meal meant friendship and acceptance. The three parables that follow answer this complaint.

f.g: Grumbled, complained under their breath.

n: Jesus responds with a parable — really a set of three stories about something lost and found.

f.g: Luke 15 contains three linked parables: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son.

n: A shepherd who loses one sheep out of a hundred leaves the ninety-nine and searches until he finds it. Every single one matters to him.

f.g: The shepherd doesn’t give up.

n: When he finds it, there is no scolding — he joyfully lifts it onto his shoulders and carries it home. This is how the Good Shepherd treats the lost.
He gathers friends and neighbors to celebrate with him. Finding the lost is a joy meant to be shared.

f.g: Notice the shepherd’s joy is the center of the story.

n: Heaven rejoices more over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who think they need no repentance — a pointed word to the self-righteous critics.

f.w: joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth

f.g: Righteous people — or those who consider themselves so.

n: A woman loses one of ten silver coins. She lights a lamp in her dim house, sweeps every corner, and searches carefully until she finds it.

f.g: Greek drachma, about a day’s wage. Some think the ten coins may have been part of a dowry or headdress.
Village homes had few windows and needed a lamp even by day.

n: She too calls her friends to celebrate. The lost coin couldn’t find its way back — someone had to search for it.

f.w: the piece which I had lost
f.g: The coin didn’t wander off; it was lost through neglect or accident.

n: In the same way, the angels of God rejoice whenever a sinner repents.

f.w: joy in the presence of the angels of God

n: The third story, often called the Prodigal Son, is really about a father and two sons — each lost in a different way.

f.g: The younger represents open sinners; the elder resembles the grumbling Pharisees.

n: The younger son demands his inheritance now — essentially treating his father as already dead. The father, with painful patience, agrees.

f.w: the portion of goods that falleth to me
f.g: His share of the estate; a younger son normally received one-third.
His property, livelihood.

n: He quickly converts everything to cash, heads to a faraway land, and squanders it all on reckless, wild living.

f.g: Scattered his wealth.
Wasteful, reckless, dissolute.

n: Just as his money runs out, a severe famine hits. Now he is in desperate need.

f.g: In need, lacking necessities.

n: He hires himself out to a foreigner who sends him to feed pigs — the lowest humiliation imaginable for a Jew, since swine were unclean.

f.g: Attached himself — almost begged for work.

n: He is so hungry he envies the pigs their feed of pods, and no one gives him anything.

f.g: Would gladly have.
Carob pods — cheap animal feed eaten by people only in extreme poverty.

n: Then he “came to himself” — he woke up to reality. Even his father’s hired workers have plenty while he is starving.

f.g: A turning point: repentance begins with seeing clearly.

n: He resolves to go home and confess that he has sinned against God and against his father.

f.w: I will arise and go to my father

f.g: A reverent Jewish way of saying “against God.”

n: He plans to ask to be treated as a hired worker. He no longer feels worthy to be called a son.

f.g: Day laborers, below even household servants in security.

n: The father has been watching. Seeing him far off, he is filled with compassion and runs — undignified for an older man — to embrace and kiss his son before a word is spoken. This is Heavenly Father’s love.

f.g: Threw his arms around him.

f.w: when he was yet a great way off

n: The son begins his confession, but the father doesn’t even let him finish the part about becoming a hired servant.

f.g: Before you, against you.

n: The father restores him fully: the best robe (honor), a ring (authority and family standing), and sandals (servants went barefoot; sons wore shoes).

f.g: A signet ring signified sonship and authority.

n: He orders the fattened calf — saved for the biggest celebrations — to be prepared for a feast.

f.g: A calf specially fed for a special occasion.

n: The father explains: my son was dead and is alive; he was lost and is found. Repentance is like coming back to life.

f.w: was dead, and is alive again

n: The elder son, coming in from working the fields, hears music and dancing from the house.

f.g: Music.

n: He asks a servant what is going on rather than going straight in.

f.g: What was happening.

n: The servant explains that his brother is home safe and the father has thrown a feast.

f.g: In good health.

n: The elder brother refuses to go in. Once again the father goes out — this time to plead with his other son. He seeks both of his lost children.

f.g: Pleaded with him, urged him.

n: The elder son complains about years of slaving and obedience without even a goat for a party. He sees himself as a servant, not a son, and resents grace shown to another.

f.g: A young goat — far less than a fatted calf.

f.w: these many years do I serve thee
f.g: Literally “slave for you” — he has missed the joy of sonship.

n: He won’t even say “my brother” — only “this son of yours.” He highlights his brother’s sins and resents the celebration.

f.g: Prostitutes.
Note he distances himself from his brother.

n: The father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.” The elder son’s inheritance was never in danger.

f.w: all that I have is thine

n: We had to celebrate — your brother was dead and is alive again, lost and now found. The story ends without telling us if the elder son went in, inviting each listener to decide how they will respond.

f.g: Right, fitting.
The father gently reminds him: he is still your brother.
